title.rendered: Physical Layer Next-Generation Spectrum Security Protection Technology Based on Intrinsic Security Attributes of Wireless Communication Systems

content.rendered:
Physical Layer Next-Generation Spectrum Security Protection Technology Based on Intrinsic Security Attributes of Wireless Communication Systems

LI G, ZHOU Y, SUN Y, et al

IEEE Network

📄 PDF
🔗 DOI Link

📌 Abstract

💡 Core Contributions

  • Comprehensive assessment of security vulnerabilities in next-generation spectrum usage. This article systematically reviews the security threats faced by existing low-frequency spectrum resources (dynamic spectrum access/sharing, NOMA, etc.) and emerging high-frequency bands (millimeter wave, terahertz, optical wireless communications), categorizing them into three major types—spectrum data leakage, spectrum unauthorized occupation, and spectrum jamming and jamming attacks—thereby providing a threat modeling foundation for the subsequent construction of an endogenous security framework.
  • Proposal of a systematic classification framework for physical-layer endogenous security attributes. This article, for the first time, classifies the endogenous security attributes of wireless communication systems into four dimensions according to system components—transceivers (uniqueness, robustness, unreplicability), transmission modes (unobservability, quantum non-cloning), channels (reciprocity, spatial decorrelation, time variability), and noise and jamming (suppressibility, artificial enhancibility, simulability)—constructing a panoramic view of endogenous security attributes.
  • Design of targeted defense solutions based on endogenous security attributes. Targeting the three categories of spectrum security threats, this article maps endogenous attributes to specific defense techniques: exploiting channel reciprocity and quantum-state unobservability to achieve secret key generation; utilizing the physical unreplicability of transceivers to achieve RF fingerprinting (RFF) and physically unclonable function-based identity authentication; leveraging the bandwidth-limited characteristics of noise to design exponential modulation frequency-hopping spread spectrum active anti-jamming schemes; and integrating channel spatial decorrelation with beamforming to achieve passive jamming defense, forming a complete physical-layer spectrum security assurance framework.

🔧 Method Overview

This article, set against multi-user wireless communication scenarios, constructs a physical-layer-oriented endogenous security assurance framework. The system components encompass four layers: transceiver hardware, transmission medium (electromagnetic waves/quantum channels), wireless channels, and noise/jamming. In terms ofspectrum data leakage defense, the framework approaches from two paths: secret key generation and signal quality defense. Secret key generation based on channel reciprocity leverages channel time variability and spatial decorrelation to dynamically update keys without relying on complex cryptographic protocols or trusted third parties; quantum key distribution provides information-theoretic security guarantees through the unobservability of quantum states; furthermore, the high directivity and fast fading characteristics of millimeter wave/terahertz naturally enhance transmission unobservability, while near-field beam focusing can further spatially isolate jamming and suppress eavesdropper channel quality. Covert communication hides the communication behavior itself within noise through artificial noise injection or RIS-assisted techniques, providing a higher level of protection. In terms ofspectrum unauthorized occupation defense, the framework comprehensively employs both hardware feature-based and channel feature-based methods. RFF utilizes transceiver manufacturing deviations to form unique physical-layer identity identifiers, and PUF achieves chip-level identity verification through challenge-response protocols; the combination of the two enables layered identity verification. Channel fingerprinting exploits the location dependence of channel CSI to distinguish legitimate users from impersonation attackers, where passive schemes assess geographic location and channel characteristics via CSI, and active schemes embed authentication tags based on shared keys into signals. In terms ofspectrum jamming and jamming attack defense, active defense employs IM-FHSS technology, which conceals idle frequencies by dynamically altering signal activation states, demonstrating superior robustness against reactive, constant, and random jamming; passive defense integrates channel fingerprinting localization with directional beamforming, first determining attacker locations using CSI spatial decorrelation, then implementing jamming suppression through precise beamforming.

📊 Experimental Results

In RF fingerprinting identification experiments under real ADS-B signal environments, the RFF model employing few-shot learning techniques achieves a classification accuracy exceeding 30 labeled samplesper device class with only 90%, demonstrating the efficiency and robustness of the RFF method against unauthorized spectrum occupation in scenarios with extremely limited labeled data.

excerpt.rendered: This paper explores the intrinsic attributes of wireless communication systems as new opportunities for security design. This tutorial aims to provide a comprehensive survey of the state of the art in physical layer wireless intrinsic security technologies, covering their principles, solutions, and future research trends, to safeguard wireless security and privacy in next-generation spectrum usage.
